Content: Water is no longer something to be owned, bought and sold. Clean and safe water is available to all.

We aren't quite there yet, but we are actively working on finding balance in how our community nourishes rather than drains the resources of the earth. The watershed is starting to make sense and settle - as we've released all the old dams and nurtured the changes in how water needs to flow. We finally shifted, with great effort, the ways of dealing with overflow water runoff so that no sewage or pollution flows into the rivers in the great rains. We gather water with much more intention. Water keepers are some of the most cherished and respected roles. There is high understanding in each community and neighborhood about the ways water travels - where from and too. This became possible because of the danger and necessity brought by high and low rains - and storms after storms after storms. We've converted the knowledge of what we needed to survive to adjust how we care for water that makes the ecosystems and watersheds ready to thrive. We aren't there yet - but it is clear it is working as the many creatures of the fresh and salt-water bodies are finding clear homes and niches. There is something closer to balance. A key negotiation was in governance of the waters - the idea of who had "rights" to water had to be considered. The old laws and treaties were not sufficient to grapple with the scale of what was needed - and yet we had to move through claims, attachments, and reconcile painful histories and mistreatments. We found our way to shared water stewardship. The water is understood as sacred - and vital. It has a place in every home and place of learning - as well as in rituals and community celebrations. We've created land and water trusts that support mutual stewardship.

Our thriving future is wet. From the lush forests of Maui drawing and developing moisture across Maui Nui to the prolific swimming in the Ala Wai Canal in Honolulu (a favorite pastime for all), water is abundant and Hawai’i’s waters are healthy and abundant as well. The Hawaii State Capitol of 1965 to 2025, today, is a monument to wai and waiwai. The structure, representing a volcano, is perpetually fountaining, not lava, but water. So abundant is water that the literal spewing of wai serves as a symbolic reminder of our collective responsibility to spew waiwai – the mana’o that drove generations of stewards of collective governance to reach that point.
